extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, peer reviewers, authors, and training/course developers in biomedical publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and summarise the expected roles and specific tasks peer reviewers are asked to perform in the manuscript review process for biomedical journals; intended to inform guidance, training, and editorial policy. This is a scoping synthesis of the literature rather than a prescriptive checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficient experts in their field
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be proficient experts in their field (including training in research methods or statistics) who can evaluate the scholarly and technical content of manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: have sufficient domain expertise and methodological/statistical knowledge to assess scientific rigour. Appears as one of three items grouped under this theme. Editors often rely on reviewers' subject-matter expertise to evaluate validity beyond editorial capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dutiful/altruistic towards scientific community
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are expected to act out of a sense of scientific responsibility and duty to the community, contributing voluntarily to the scholarly enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes willingness to review without payment, recognition of reviewing as professional service. The review notes that the large number of expected tasks may overburden unpaid reviewers and that time pressures influence willingness to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar with journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be familiar with the journal’s mission, scope, and review criteria/guidelines before starting a review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: reviewers ought to check journal instructions and align their report with journal-specific expectations (e.g., whether to assess novelty/clinical relevance or follow a structured report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbiased and ethical professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be unbiased and adhere to ethical norms (declare or avoid conflicts of interest, maintain confidentiality, avoid discriminatory or prestige-based biases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of biases: prestige, affiliation, nationality, language, gender, content-based, confirmation, conservatism, interdisciplinarity bias, publication bias. Guidance: declare conflicts up front or avoid reviewing; maintain confidentiality; be aware of multiple bias sources. Many statements (18 items) support this theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-critical professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be self-critical about their competence and availability and only accept reviews when able to perform them adequately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before accepting, reviewers should assess if they have time and appropriate expertise. This reduces low-quality or rushed reviews and addresses the problem of disproportionate reviewing load within the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliable professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be dependable: meet deadlines, deliver reports in a timely manner, and follow through on agreed commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is emphasised as vital; late or non-delivered reviews burden editorial workflows. Reliability also covers consistent adherence to ethical and procedural expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should act as skilled critics who provide objective, thorough, specific, and constructive criticism to improve manuscripts’ scientific content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was one of the most frequent themes (15 items). Guidance: focus on scientific content, methods, interpretation, and validity rather than merely stylistic issues; be specific and actionable. Avoid vague comments (e.g., 'check adequacy of abstract') without detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful communicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must communicate politely and collegially, offering feedback in a tone that promotes education and constructive improvement of authors’ work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polite, collegial attitude supports educational function. Reports should be constructive, avoid personal attacks, and help authors revise. Tone matters for uptake and the educational role of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeepers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers serve a gatekeeping function by helping to filter manuscripts for scientific quality and appropriateness for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gatekeeping overlaps with editorial responsibilities; the review highlights tension because editors make final decisions yet reviewer recommendations heavily influence outcomes. Reviewers should be mindful they are advisors, not final decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers have an educational role: to help authors improve manuscripts and to mentor through constructive comments and suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers can contribute to developing authors’ skills; the paper suggests using open reports and 'snippets' for training. Educational comments should be focused and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocates for author/editor/reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Some literature expects reviewers to act as advocates for one or more stakeholders (authors, editors, or readers), though this role is debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'advocate' is ambiguous and may conflict with objectivity. The review questions whether one can simultaneously advocate for different stakeholders and calls for clarification of priorities if advocacy is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisors to editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should advise editors on the merits of manuscripts (including recommendations on accept/reject) while recognising that editors make final publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: provide reasoned recommendations and assessments of strengths/weaknesses, but remember editorial independence. The review points out that reviewer recommendations can unduly influence editorial decisions and that role boundaries should be clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles not within the remit of peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature identifies certain roles/tasks that generally fall outside reviewers’ remit (e.g., full responsibility for detecting fraud, some aspects of copy editing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/controversies: detecting fraud often requires raw data access and is impractical; many argue fraud detection and addressing allegations should be editor responsibilities. Copy editing is usually not expected, though some sources request grammatical corrections; excessive copyediting is discouraged due to time costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation and approach to reviewing (task theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks relating to how reviewers organise and approach the review process (e.g., plan review, check conflicts, assess own competence, follow journal structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theme contains 10 task items. Guidance includes: assess availability and competence before accepting; familiarise with journal guidelines; use a structured approach; disclose conflicts; prioritise scientific content over copy editing; manage time efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make general comments (task theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks involving high-level, overall comments on the manuscript (e.g., summary of main findings, overall strengths and weaknesses, significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains 10 items. Reviewers should provide an overall assessment summarising key messages and major concerns, focusing on clarity, significance, novelty, and overall suitability for the journal. Avoid vague high-level remarks without actionable detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and address content for each section of the manuscript (task theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks to evaluate and comment on each manuscript section (title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusions) and their coherence, validity, and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Largest theme (36 items). Includes evaluating study question, design, methods (including statistics), data presentation, interpretation, conclusions, and whether claims are supported. Note: authors excluded tasks specific to RCTs or systematic reviews in their extraction; journals differ in whether they expect reviewers to assess novelty/clinical relevance as well as methodological rigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address ethical aspects (task theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks focused on ethical issues: assessing conflicts of interest, plagiarism, ethical approval, participant consent, and possible misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five items in this theme. Guidance: reviewers should flag ethical concerns and possible misconduct, but detecting fraud/plagiarism may be limited by lack of access to raw data and tools—editors/publishers often have more resources (e.g., plagiarism detection software). There is disagreement on extent of reviewer responsibility here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess manuscript presentation (task theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks related to the manuscript’s presentation: clarity, organisation, readability, figures/tables, adherence to reporting guidelines, and formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eight items in this theme. Guidance: reviewers should comment on clarity and structure but not be expected to perform detailed copy editing. Reports should note presentation problems that impede assessment of scientific content; suggest adherence to reporting standards (e.g., CONSORT) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide recommendations (task theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks to offer explicit recommendations to the editor (e.g., accept, revise, reject) and actionable suggestions for authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four items in this theme. Guidance: recommendations should be supported by specific rationale and linked to identified strengths/weaknesses. The review cautions that recommendations influence editorial decisions and editors should be aware of potential undue influence; reviewers remain advisors, not final decision-makers.
